newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania orders seizure of pyramid scheme cash.
newsitem.headline: Albania orders seizure of pyramid scheme cash.

text.p: The Albanian government, responding to protests over crumbling get-rich-quick investment schemes, on Thursday ordered the seizure of millions of dollars deposited in state-owned banks, Albanian television reported.
Demonstrations against collapsing pyramid investment schemes spread beyond Tirana on Thursday to the western city of Vlore and Shkoder in the north, state media reported.

Large numbers of police were deployed around the Albanian capital itself to prevent a repeat of clashes on Wednesday when thousands of angry savers took to the streets to demand money back from Sude, once one of the most popular of the schemes.
In a swift response, the government had ordered the seizure of 25.5 billion leks ($255 million) deposited in banks, television said.

"In order to avoid the consequences, (and) bearing in mind the pyramid character of the Sude company...the Albanian government has decided to freeze a total of $25 billion leks deposited by the schemes for the benefit of Albanian citizens," said the television report quoting from a government statement.
It said government sequestration would continue until a parliamentary committee has studied each investment and ruled on whether it was a pyramid scheme.
"The government orders competent bodies (the two state-owned banks) not to conduct banking transactions for companies which do not pay their own creditors," it added.

The decision may just be enough to take the fire out of mounting protests and satisfy investors who had feared losing all their savings. The ruling may also sound the death-knell of pyramid schemes in Albania although opposition parties say the investments have already damaged the impoverished economy.
The schemes, which seduced Albanians into selling everything they owned with promises of big returns on small outlays, mushroomed after the fall of communism in 1990.

In Tirana on Wednesday, President Sali Berisha's conservative Democratic Party bore some of the the brunt of disappointed investors' ire, where the Sude bankruptcy has left thousands out of pocket in Europe's poorest country.

As a precaution against further protests, police were on Thursday stationed in and around the city's main Skanderbeg Square, scene of anti-government demonstrations last year, and at key road junctions, witnesses said.

But in Vlore, 150 km (90 miles) west of Tirana, protesters hurled stones at the city hall in fury that a local firm called Gjallica had postponed resuming payments to depositors, Radio Tirana reported.
"People headed to the city hall. They shouted slogans against the government and threw stones and other objects which damaged the building," the radio said.
State television painted a similar picture in the northern city of Shkoder, where it described the atmosphere as "tense".
The first shoots of fresh unrest in Albania coincided with a call for mass protests from the opposition Socialists, heirs to the former communists.

The appeal appears to have gone unheard but some newspapers echoed the sentiment. In a commentary, the independent newspaper Koha Jone said the moment had come to mirror unrest in fellow Balkan states Serbia and Bulgaria.
